name: Spiral of silence
statement: People who sense their view is losing ground say less about it, so the opinion that looks dominant grows louder and its rival drops out of public view.
meaning: The theory joins two claims of different sizes. The small one is about a person: someone who reads the climate of opinion as hostile to their own view becomes less willing to voice it, out of fear of isolation rather than out of doubt. The large one is about a society: because everyone is reading everyone else, small differences in who speaks compound over time, and one side is established as public opinion while the other falls silent. Noelle-Neumann's definition follows from the second claim. Public opinion is the opinion that can be voiced without fear of sanction. Nearly all the empirical work tests the first claim, at one moment, with a survey question, and the gap between what is claimed and what is measured is the subject of most of the argument about the theory.

origin.note: Her article is a condensed version of a longer German paper in a Festschrift for Arnold Gehlen, which carried 33 tables of survey results. The English-language book, The Spiral of Silence: Public Opinion, Our Social Skin, followed from the University of Chicago Press in 1984, translated from Die Schweigespirale.

evidence: Noelle-Neumann drew on Allensbach institute surveys run mostly in 1971 and 1972, each with 1,000 to 2,000 interviews on a representative cross-section of West Germans. Twelve controversial topics were put to respondents, from abortion law to recognition of the GDR. Willingness to speak was measured by asking people to imagine a conversation among passengers on a long train journey and to say whether they would join in. Across 9,966 respondents, 36% said they would discuss the topic, 51% would not and 13% were undecided. The central table concerns socialism in August 1972. Among people who thought socialism would establish itself and welcomed it, 53% would join the train conversation; among those who thought the same and feared it, 28% would. The pattern held separately among the politically interested and the uninterested. Two of the twelve topics ran the other way. On the treaties with Moscow and Warsaw, and on more influence for Franz Josef Strauss, minorities of 17 to 25% were at least as willing to speak as majorities of 53 to 61%, which Noelle-Neumann read as a hard core that has grown used to isolation.

replication.headline: The individual-level correlation turns up again and again and is tiny; the spiral itself is rarely tested, and where it has been it runs in opposite directions in different countries.
replication.detail: Matthes, Knoll and von Sikorski pooled 66 studies with more than 27,000 participants and report r = .10 between perceived opinion support and political opinion expression. They found the relationship no weaker online than offline, and no variation by the number or opinion of the people being addressed, by climate characteristics, or by design, measurement and sample features. The largest silencing effect, r = .34, came when people talked to family, friends or neighbours about obtrusive issues. Their reading is that the relationship is stronger and more robust than previously thought, which is a comparison with the earlier meta-analysis by Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan. That 1997 paper is paywalled and was not read here. Xu, Liu, Kim and Chon give its figure as an average r = 0.054 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.028 to 0.080, and that number reaches this page through them rather than through the paper. Both meta-analyses cover the static micro test only. Thurre, Gale and Staerklé went at the macro claim instead, using eight rounds of the European Social Survey from 2002 to 2016 across 15 countries and 195,194 respondents, with signing petitions, displaying stances and joining demonstrations as the dependent variable. Pro-immigration opinion was associated with speaking out in all 15 countries, but the direction of movement over 14 years split: pro-immigration voices lost ground in France, Ireland and Switzerland and gained it in Germany, Hungary, Poland and the UK. Their conclusion is that a single time point cannot diagnose a spiral, and that a carefully timed static test would still have reached misleading conclusions in several of those countries.

study.cite: Matthes, J., Knoll, J., & von Sikorski, C. (2018). The "spiral of silence" revisited: A meta-analysis on the relationship between perceptions of opinion support and political opinion expression. Communication Research, 45(1), 3-33.

limits: The train question asks what a person imagines they would do, and no validation of it against observed behaviour was located, in Crossref searches or in the reference lists of the papers read here. The two studies that come closest changed the answer. Hayes, Shanahan and Glynn gave people six topics to discuss with a real group they expected to meet, and report a relationship much larger than the meta-analytic average, without saying in the abstract how much larger. Hayes, Uldall and Glynn staged actual conversations with trained confederates who produced a climate either agreeing or disagreeing with the participant, and found the climate moved expression only among people who scored high on the Willingness to Self-Censor Scale. Glynn, Hayes and Shanahan's meta-analysis could not be obtained, so its pooled figure, its study count and its moderator tests are all reported here at second hand or not at all. Thurre and colleagues flag social desirability as a rival explanation for their pro-immigration results, and note that their outspokenness measure is generic rather than tied to the specific issue.
misreadings: The famous version of the train test has a five-hour journey in it. The 1974 article describes only a conversation among passengers on a long train journey and puts no length on it. The theory is also cited as though it predicted uniform silencing, which its own first paper does not: two of the twelve topics produced a minority more willing to speak than the majority, and Noelle-Neumann said so. Pew Research Center's 2014 study is the most quoted modern evidence and is widely described as showing that social media silences people. It surveyed 1,801 American adults between 7 August and 16 September 2013 about the Snowden surveillance disclosures, and asked what they would be willing to say, not what they had said. Of those asked, 86% were willing to discuss the story in person and 42% of Facebook and Twitter users were willing to post about it; of the 14% unwilling to discuss it in person, 0.3% would post about it. That is a difference between two hypothetical willingness measures. The pooled correlation is the other trap. An r of .10 across 66 studies is a real relationship and a weak predictor of any individual's behaviour, and it is evidence for the conformity step rather than for the spiral the theory is named after.
